notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Job 12, compiled from the sources I could reach. I note where certain traditions or viewpoints were unavailable.

---

## Job 12 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

Job replies to Zophar (who had just spoken in ch. 11). It is a sarcastic opening (vv. 1–3), a lament that the righteous are mocked while the wicked prosper (vv. 4–6), an appeal to creation as witness to God's sovereignty (vv. 7–12), and a sweeping hymn on God's irresistible power over all human affairs (vv. 13–25). The speech continues through ch. 14.

---

### v. 1 — "Then Job answered:"

All sources agree this begins Job's reply to Zophar's first speech (Job 11). Each of the three friends has now spoken once, and Job answers the third. (Ellicott)

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm
- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

---

### v. 2 — "Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!"

**Traditional reading:** Biting sarcasm. Job's friends have acted as if they alone possess wisdom and when they die, all wisdom will vanish from the earth. (EnduringWord / Guzik)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill expands: "ye are the people" is deeply ironic — they behave as if they are the only wise and important people in the world, monopolising knowledge. "Wisdom shall die with you" also reminds them that, wise as they think they are, they must die, and their worldly wisdom will come to nothing. Yet true wisdom, made known by God, will always abide.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Grant (Brethren) notes that Zophar had implied he had intuitive wisdom that Job lacked, and Job rightly reproves him.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 3 — "But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?"

**Traditional reading:** Job makes two points: (1) he too has understanding and is not intellectually or spiritually inferior to them; (2) the theological principles Zophar has presented are widely known commonplaces, not deep secrets. (EnduringWord / Guzik)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill notes the Hebrew for "understanding" is literally "heart" — Job claims a wise and understanding heart, a new heart, sincere and upright. "I am not inferior to you" means he is not falling before them as one defeated or intimidated; nor has he fallen from God as an apostate as they insinuated. The things they have presented as deep mysteries are common notions everyone knows — for instance, that God made the world and governs it.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) notes: "To claim superior knowledge over others is always offensive. To do so against a sick and broken man from the vantage-ground of health and prosperity is nothing less than a cruelty."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/12.htm

Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "I would we had another Job, to chastise the high-sounding language of modern theologians."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

---

### v. 4 — "I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered. The righteous and upright man is a laughingstock."

**Traditional reading:** Job complains that though he was a godly man — one who called on God and received answer — and though he was "just and blameless," he is now ridiculed by his own friends. This is a key counter-example to the friends' theology that the righteous are always blessed. (EnduringWord / Guzik)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill: Job instances himself to prove that good men are afflicted. He was once prosperous and caressed by all; now he is the scorn of friends. "Mocked of his neighbour" (or "friend") aggravates the affliction (cf. Psalm 55:12). He was mocked not merely by profane men but by a professing believer who called on God. "The just upright man" — truly righteous, upright in heart — becomes a laughingstock.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Ellicott: "The laughing-stock of his companion — he who called on God, and He answered him." This is either the character Job claims for himself, or the supposed taunt of his friends. Ellicott adds: "Ridicule is no test of truth or of merit."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

Guzik draws a parallel to Christ: Jesus was mocked by soldiers (Matt. 27:29), chief priests (Matt. 27:41), and others (Mark 15:27–31), making Job a type of the suffering righteous one.

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

---

### v. 5 — "The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping."

**Traditional reading:** Those who are comfortable and prosperous look with contempt on the calamity of others. The BSB rendering "scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping" reflects the idea that the prosperous see disaster as something deserved by those who are unsteady.

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill: "He that is ready to slip with his feet" refers to one falling into calamities — Job means himself. Such a person is "as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease" — when the lamp of prosperity burns bright, a man is valued; when it is dim or extinguished, he is despised.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Ellicott notes the KJV rendering "Is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease" conveys no clear sense. He offers two readings: (a) the lamp or torch prepared for tottering feet in darkness is disregarded by those at ease who need no such aid; or (b) more probably, "there is contempt for calamity in the thoughts of him that is at ease; it is ready at hand for them who are tottering with their feet."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

---

### v. 6 — "The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure — those who carry their god in their hands."

**Traditional reading:** Job's experience now seems upside-down: the wicked prosper while he, the righteous man, suffers. This directly contradicts the friends' simplistic retribution theology. (EnduringWord / Guzik) Guzik quotes Chambers: "Job's creed has crumbled into ruins, 'therefore', he says, 'I leave my creed, but I deny that I have left God.'"

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill: "The tabernacles of robbers prosper" — perhaps Job has in mind the Chaldeans and Sabeans who robbed him. "They that provoke God are secure" — living in tranquillity despite grievous, God-provoking sins. Gill notes the alternative reading of the final clause: "who makes a god with his hand" or "carries a god in his hand" — referring to idol-worshippers who carry their idols (as some Hebrew interpreters take it).

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Ellicott likewise notes the alternative: "to him that bringeth his god in his hand" (cf. Habakkuk 1:11, 16) though he thinks "into whose hand God bringeth abundantly" fits usage better.

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

Grant suggests Job is hinting that his friends themselves are like prospering robbers — they are stealing his integrity and provoking God while pretending to speak for Him, yet they remain secure.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 7 — "But ask the animals, and they will instruct you; ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you."

**Traditional reading:** Job tells his friends that what they have been saying about God is so elementary that even the brute beasts know it. Creation itself teaches God's sovereignty. (EnduringWord / Guzik) Guzik quotes Mason: "Even a dog has more knowledge of God than you do!"

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill: Even from irrational creatures one can learn that God is the Maker, Sustainer, and Disposer of all things. Or, more specifically to the point in dispute, the creatures illustrate that the harmless and useful are often preyed upon while predators roam unmolested (Habakkuk 1:13) — a pattern contradicting the friends' neat theology.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

---

### v. 8 — "Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; let the fish of the sea inform you."

Gill notes that "speak to the earth" can be rendered "ask a sprig of the earth" — any shrub or tree — and it will teach that all things are raised and preserved by God's power.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Grant: Job appeals to all creation — beasts, birds, earth, fish — as witnesses to the Creator's power and greatness, showing far more than Zophar did about God.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 9 — "Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?"

**Key observation — the Divine Name:** This is the only place in the poetic dialogue sections of Job where the covenant name **Yahweh** (LORD) appears. None of the three friends ever use it; only Job does. This is taken by multiple commentators as evidence of Job's superior knowledge of God.

- Ellicott: "Job's very use of the word in such a context is the clearest evidence of the superior knowledge that he claims. No one of his friends makes use of the name; but Job uses it here, and shows thereby his knowledge of the covenant name." — **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

- EnduringWord / Guzik: quotes Andersen — "its rarity makes it so conspicuous." — **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

- Gill likewise notes this is the only place "Jehovah" is used by the disputants in the book. — **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

---

### v. 10 — "The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the breath of all mankind."

Gill: The life (soul) of every brute creature comes from God and continues by His will. "The breath of all mankind" — originally breathed into man by God (Gen. 2:7); it remains in His hand. Even the breath of kings is in God's hand (cf. Daniel 5:23). The Hebrew reads "the spirit of all the flesh of men" — the rational soul.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Grant: Job affirms that the breath of all mankind — not only his own but that of his three friends — is in God's hand. They cannot stand as detached onlookers judging matters without being judged themselves.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 11 — "Does not the ear test words as the tongue tastes its food?"

**Traditional reading:** Just as the palate instinctively discriminates between sweet and bitter, so the ear (and mind) tests and evaluates what it hears. Job is saying he has exercised his own judgment on their words and found them wanting. (EnduringWord / Guzik, quoting Meyer: "There is no appeal from the verdict of our palate.")

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Gill: Those with spiritual ears test the words of God and men, distinguishing true from false. Those whose taste is changed relish spiritual things — they "taste that the Lord is gracious." Job means the things his friends said are as easy to test as sounds by the ear or food by the mouth.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Ellicott: Bildad had appealed to the wisdom of authority and tradition (Job 8:8–10), but Job reminds him that the wise man must discriminate, not accept everything received. "He allows that wisdom is the prerogative of age, but reminds him that the Ancient of Days must needs be wise indeed."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

---

### v. 12 — "Wisdom is found with the elderly, and understanding comes with long life."

**Traditional reading:** This is another truism — normally, age brings wisdom. But Job may be quoting his friends ironically or using it as a transition: if wisdom is with the aged, then how much more wisdom belongs to the eternal God (the "Ancient of Days"). (Gill, Ellicott, EnduringWord)

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

**Alternative reading (modern/evangelical):** Constable (Expository Notes) suggests Job 12:12 may be irony — this is not what Job himself believes. Or Job may be asking a rhetorical question: "Is wisdom with aged men…?" The point being that God alone is truly wise (v. 13), in refutation of Bildad's appeal to the ancients (Job 8:8).

- **URL:** https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-12.html

Grant: Job sets Zophar's professed wisdom aside — wisdom is with aged men indeed, and God is the most ancient of all; therefore true wisdom resides with Him.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 13 — "Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His."

**Traditional reading:** Job now launches into his own hymn of God's greatness, directly answering Zophar's implication (Job 11:7–12) that Job does not know God. Job demonstrates he knows God's attributes very well indeed. God possesses wisdom and power together — in ancient Near Eastern myths these qualities often resided in different gods, not one. (EnduringWord / Guzik; Constable)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/
- **URL:** https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-12.html

---

### v. 14 — "What He tears down cannot be rebuilt; the man He imprisons cannot be released."

Guzik quotes Clarke: "He alone can create, and he alone can destroy. Nothing can be annihilated but by the same Power that created it." This shows God's power over material things and over men — when God acts, no human can reverse it.

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Ellicott: "God has equal power over the moral and physical world."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

Grant observes: Job himself had been broken down, but he didn't realise that the One who broke him down could also rebuild him, though Job could not. If God imprisons, man cannot release — though God can.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 15 — "If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land."

God's power over nature — drought and flood alike are in His hand. Grant notes that these two extremes have often followed one another and men are helpless, though God does not explain why He does this.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 16 — "True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His."

**Traditional reading:** God has power over minds — both the deceived and the deceiver are under His sovereign control. Gill notes this in passing.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

Guzik categorises this under God's power "over minds."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Grant: Job gives God credit for this without realising its significance for his own case — both the deceived and deceiver are under God's control, meaning God is sovereign even over the deceptions Job has suffered.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 17 — "He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges."

**Traditional reading:** God humbles the wisest human advisors. "Barefoot" (or "plundered" in some translations) pictures counselors stripped of their dignity and led away as captives. Judges, esteemed for wisdom, are made fools. (EnduringWord / Guzik; Grant)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/
- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

Grant: "He deprives counsellors of the value of their counsel: thus man's wisdom is brought to nothing, and the judges become foolish: man's authority becomes as useless as his wisdom."

---

### v. 18 — "He loosens the bonds placed by kings and fastens a belt around their waists."

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott gives two interpretations: (a) God loosens the confederacy or alliance by which kings bind themselves together, and girds them (with a belt) to fight against each other; or (b) the "belt" is the girdle of servitude, contrasting with the royal girdle of state. Either way, God sovereignly humbles rulers.

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

---

### v. 19 — "He leads priests away barefoot and overthrows the established."

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word can mean either "princes" or "priests." Here the parallelism seems to suit "princes" better, though some translations read "priests." Either way, God overthrows even the seemingly most established and secure.

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

---

### v. 20 — "He deprives the trusted of speech and takes away the discernment of elders."

Grant: "Those who have been considered dependable are deprived of speech, the ability to be of help to others, and even elders who have been recognised for their experience will find their discernment taken away."

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

Guzik categorises this under God's power "over the eloquent."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

---

### v. 21 — "He pours out contempt on nobles and disarms the mighty."

Guzik notes the Hebrew for "disarms the mighty" is literally "loosens the belt of the mighty" — an idiom for depriving someone of strength, because loosened garments hinder the movement needed for combat (quoting Bullinger).

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Grant: "To princes (those in the place of dignity) God sees fit to show contempt, so contrary to what they might expect. The powerful He disarms, taking their power from them."

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

---

### v. 22 — "He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings deep shadows into light."

**Traditional reading:** God uncovers hidden things. He brings to light what is concealed in darkness and even what lies in "the shadow of death." (EnduringWord / Guzik; Grant)

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Grant makes a poignant application: Job was experiencing the pangs of darkness and could not himself uncover deep things from it — but he realised God can. "Could He not do it in Job's case? Yes indeed, and He did so before long."

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

Constable (Expository Notes) notes: "Man can only understand God's ways by special revelation from God. His ways are inscrutable."

- **URL:** https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-12.html

---

### v. 23 — "He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them."

Ellicott expands on this verse at length: "The latter part of this chapter teaches us a truth that is apt to be forgotten … Why is it that the counsel of the wisest sometimes faileth … but because there is One working underneath it all for His own ends and to His own glory." He notes that Zophar, with all his common sense, had scarcely risen to the perception of this truth — that God's dealings are inscrutable and from their very darkness suggest the necessity for faith. Job's conception of God's righteous government "far transcended that of his friends."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

Guzik categorises this under God's power "over the nations."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

---

### v. 24 — "He deprives the earth's leaders of reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland."

Guzik: "This shows how easy it is for God to make men wander … All He must do is merely take away understanding, showing that the wisdom and understanding of man is dependent upon God."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

---

### v. 25 — "They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards."

**Traditional reading — Job describes himself:** Multiple commentators suggest that in these final verses Job is unconsciously describing his own condition. Guzik: "We sense that Job actually described himself, as this prominent man without understanding, a man wandering in a pathless wilderness, a man groping in the dark without light, and who staggered like a drunken man."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

Ellicott: "Job is thus the type of a man who has felt the hollowness and unreality of traditional orthodoxy, and is feeling his way in thick darkness, sustained, nevertheless, by an unquenchable faith that there is light, and that the light will eventually dawn. That this character is the more acceptable to the God of truth is made abundantly clear in the sequel."

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Observations

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (EnduringWord / David Guzik)

Guzik, who comes from a charismatic evangelical background, emphasises the experiential dimension: Job's "creed has crumbled" yet he does not abandon God; even in spiritual darkness one can cling to God's sovereignty. Guzik also makes a strong typological link to Christ's mocking (v. 4). He stresses the application that "when our former understanding of God has crumbled … we can still cling to the truth that God is sovereignly wise and mighty."

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-12/

### Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)

Piper does not comment verse-by-verse on Job 12 in the available pages, but his overall framework for Job stresses that God is sovereign over all suffering, that He permits Satan to bring calamity to prove and purify faith, and that "Satan does not have the last word." Job's friends represent "misapplied theology" — true theology distorted out of proportion. This framework shapes how a Reformed Baptist would read Job 12: Job's complaints about God's inscrutable power are not final truth but part of the struggle toward eventual revelation.

- **URL:** https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-should-i-read-the-book-of-job
- **URL:** https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/whats-true-and-false-in-job

### Brethren (Grant's Commentary)

L. M. Grant takes a devotional approach, repeatedly noting that Job states truths about God without applying them to his own case — a pattern that would have helped Job if he had reflected on it. For example, Job says God "uncovers deep things out of darkness" (v. 22) but does not yet trust that God will do this for him.

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-12.html

### Anglican (Ellicott)

Ellicott gives careful attention to translation issues (e.g., vv. 5, 9, 18, 19). He highlights the unique use of "Jehovah" in v. 9, the alternative readings of vv. 6 and 18, and the broader theological point that Job's view of God's inscrutable providence is actually more advanced than his friends' tidy retribution scheme.

- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/12.htm

### Older Baptist (Gill)

Gill provides the most detailed word-by-word exposition. He gives the Hebrew textual alternatives (e.g., "heart" for understanding in v. 3; "carries a god in his hand" for v. 6b) and spiritualises many phrases (e.g., v. 11: the "ear" and "mouth" as pictures of spiritual discernment; v. 12 as pointing toward God as the Ancient of Days). He is the only source I retrieved that explicitly reads v. 6b as possibly referring to idol-worshippers.

- **URL:** https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/12.htm

---

## Gaps — What I Could Not Find

- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org):** No verse-by-verse Job 12 material surfaced in my searches.
- **Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com):** No specific Job 12 commentary found.
- **Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox (oca.org):** No Job 12 commentary retrieved.
- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org):** Not retrieved. Peake's Commentary (early 20th c. critical scholarship) was partially available — it notes that Duhm regards v. 11 as the start of the genuine speech of Job, with v. 12 as a quotation of the friends: "With aged men, ye say, is wisdom." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-12.html)
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace:** No material from those traditions on Job 12 surfaced in the searches I could run.
- **Spurgeon (spurgeon.org):** Only a brief quote from Spurgeon (via Guzik) was found: "I would we had another Job, to chastise the high-sounding language of modern theologians." No dedicated Spurgeon sermon on Job 12 was retrieved.
